newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Tennis-British wonderboy faces test of class against Chang.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Tennis-British wonderboy faces test of class against Chang.

text.p: Long-suffering British tennis fans find out on Friday whether their latest standard-bearer can really lead them to glory, or if he's just a nice young man from Oxford headed to another false dawn.
Two weeks into the year, 22-year-old Tim Henman has made two tour finals and captured his first tour title. He is in the unlikely position, for a Briton, of heading the 1997 win lists.
But if it's just a lucky roll he's on then Henman will be found out when he takes to centre court against world number two Michael Chang in the Australian Open third round on Friday.

The clean-cut son of an Oxford lawyer -- a kind of Hugh Grant without the glasses or girlfriends -- Henman earned national adoration at Wimbledon last year when he became the first homegrown male to reach the quarter-finals for 23 years.
On his way he beat world number four Yevgeny Kafelnikov, the tireless Russian who had just won at Roland Garros.
More big wins followed and in Sydney last week he ousted world number three Goran Ivanisevic, much to the displeasure of the volatile Croat.
Henman's world ranking after the Sydney title rose to 14, making him the first Briton in the top 20 since Buster Mottram in 1983.

But on Friday evening against Chang, Henman meets a player who is a class up from anyone he has ever beaten. At his best, the 24-year-old from Hoboken, New Jersey, is a genius. And with his last grand slam title dating back to the 1989 French Open, Chang is hungry.
Henman beware. Comparisons with Fred Perry, Britain's last great tennis champion back in the days of long, white trousers, are premature.

After beating Richey Reneberg on Wednesday, Chang said he would need to play his most precise game to beat Henman, a serve-and-volley specialist who obviously enjoys taking risks. The two men have never played each other.
Chang is more the baseline type, although his serve has grown in power in recent years and he does not flinch from coming forward if his foes begin to falter.
Henman and his "barmy army" of fans in Melbourne relish what is easily the most intriguing fixture yet in the year's first grand slam.
"I feel that if I can be aggressive, then maybe I can be the dictator," Henman said after earning the tie against Chang.
Maybe. But England's patient tennis-lovers should keep the elderflower champagne on ice just a little longer.
